concepts.plain: **At-least-once**: a message may repeat, never be lost. Exactly-once *delivery* over a network that drops acknowledgements is impossible; systems give exactly-once **effect**: repeats made harmless.
concepts.analogy: A courier who redelivers whenever unsure you signed: you never miss a parcel, sometimes you get two.
concepts.why: A6's consumers are all at-least-once; dual-write producers can also lose. Its stacks, **N** (naive), **K** (Kafka transactions), **I** (key at the sink) and **O+I** (outbox plus key), differ in where, and whether, repeats are made harmless.

concepts.plain: A consumer's progress in a partition is an **offset**: the next position to read. A6's consumers commit it only after their Postgres commit, so a crash in between means the batch is redelivered from the old offset.
concepts.analogy: A bookmark moved only after you finish the chapter: fall asleep first and you reread the chapter.
concepts.why: That gap is the **commit window**. Cell F4-con-t kills a consumer exactly there; on N it is the detection gate's planted duplicate.

concepts.plain: An **idempotent producer** lets the broker drop a retried batch it already wrote, within one producer session; a restarted process or a relay re-sending is new to it. A Kafka **transaction** commits Kafka writes and consumer offsets atomically; Postgres is not a participant.
concepts.why: So K can still apply a batch twice: die between its Postgres commit and `commitTransaction`, and the batch is redelivered while the Postgres commit stands. A6's H1 tests this.

concepts.plain: A group splits partitions among live members. One silent past `session.timeout.ms` loses them and a new **generation** starts; an offset commit from an old generation is rejected: **generation fencing**. A **zombie**, paused and woken with a batch in hand, can still write outside Kafka.
concepts.analogy: A worker dozes off holding a task; it is reassigned. He wakes and finishes it anyway, and only his timesheet is rejected.
concepts.why: Cell F5 makes one. In reconnaissance on N it wrote its batch to Postgres, then failed its offset commit, in all 17 F5 trials. On K, **epoch fencing** does not apply: each instance has its own `transactional.id`.

concepts.term: The dual write, and the outbox
concepts.plain: Commit the database, then send to Kafka: two commits in two systems. A crash or send timeout between them leaves a recorded payment never published. The **outbox** writes the payment and an 'event to publish' row in one transaction; a relay (Debezium, reading the database log) publishes it later, **at least once**.
concepts.analogy: Diary, then a text to a friend: if the phone dies in between, the friend never hears. The outbox writes the text in the diary; a courier sends it, maybe twice.
concepts.why: N, K and I dual-write; cell F4-svc kills the service right after its source commit. O+I's outbox moves duplicates downstream rather than removing them, so it still needs the key.

concepts.plain: A unique `payment_id`, assigned at the origin, inserted into a `processed` table in **the same transaction** as the balance update: a repeat conflicts and is skipped. It breaks if the key is made downstream, or check and write are separate transactions.
concepts.analogy: A ticket barcode printed at purchase and scanned at the gate: a second scan is refused. A barcode printed at the gate would defeat it.
concepts.why: Why not dedupe by Kafka offset? A relay's re-send lands at a **new** offset; only a key carried from the origin catches it. I and O+I bet on this key.

concepts.term: Checking a history: ok, fail, info
concepts.plain: Jepsen-style, record each request as **ok**, **fail** (here: provably never reached the service) or **info** (a timeout or 5xx: may or may not have happened). With unique IDs and commuting increments, counting each ID in source, topic and apply log is a complete check.
concepts.analogy: A payment page that timed out: the money may or may not have gone; only the statement says.
concepts.why: A6's source database is the authority and resolves every info. The apply log keeps each apply's `(partition, offset)`: same offset means a redelivery, a new offset a re-send.

concepts.term: Real faults, and checking they landed
concepts.plain: **SIGKILL** ends a process with no cleanup. **`docker pause`** freezes it; it wakes unaware time passed. A Toxiproxy **blackhole** keeps a connection open and drops the bytes; disabling a proxy instead resets connections, which fail fast: a different fault. The seed fixes the **schedule**, not the outcome.
concepts.why: A **manipulation check**, reading only orchestrator, broker and process state, confirms each A6 trial's fault took effect. A trial is void if not, and never because of what the checker found.

concepts.plain: A zero means something only if the harness can see a nonzero. A **positive control** runs a case that must produce the anomaly; a **negative control**, one that must produce none.
concepts.analogy: Testing a smoke alarm with test smoke before trusting its silence.
concepts.why: A6's detection gate, run before the campaign, planted a duplicate and a loss on N only, ran no-fault trials on every stack and tested the checker on synthetic histories. It passed.

views.title: Where a duplicate can enter
views.caption: Two routes repeat a payment: the [outbox relay](p3:dualwrite) re-reading after a crash, at a new offset, and [redelivery](p3:offsets) to a restarted consumer, at the same offset. The [producer](p3:idempotence)'s own retries are dropped by the broker. The [key](p3:key) is checked last.

recall.q: A consumer is killed after its Postgres commit but before its offset commit. What happens on restart?
recall.a: It resumes from the last committed offset, so the batch is redelivered and applied again: an extra apply at the same (partition, offset), unless the sink checks a key.

recall.q: Why is a Kafka offset a bad idempotency key under an outbox relay?
recall.a: After a crash the relay re-reads and re-sends, and the copy lands at a new offset: to an offset key it is a new message. A key assigned at the origin is the same on every copy.

recall.q: K commits its offsets inside a Kafka transaction. How can it still apply a payment twice?
recall.a: Its Postgres commit is outside the transaction. Die after it and before `commitTransaction`: the transaction aborts on restart, the batch is redelivered, the Postgres commit stands.

recall.q: A zombie consumer wakes with a batch in hand. Which fencing stops it, and does that stop the duplicate?
recall.a: Generation fencing, at its offset commit. Its Postgres write is another system's commit and has already happened, so fencing stops the Kafka commit, not the ledger write.

recall.q: Why is a timed-out request recorded as info, not fail?
recall.a: It may have reached the service and been recorded. Calling it fail would turn real deliveries into false anomalies; in A6 the source database resolves it, which a real client cannot do.

recall.q: A cell shows zero duplicates. What must hold before that zero means anything?
recall.a: The checker must be able to see a duplicate (a positive control that produced one), and the fault must have taken effect in each trial (its manipulation check).
